sub: Technology block (c): asynchronous communication between the systems that must never wait for each other

title: Why Message Queues?
desc: A system for asynchronous communication between applications

items: Asynchronous communication: the sender does not wait for the receiver
In the Java world specified by JMS (Java Message Service), part of Java/Jakarta EE
Supports loose coupling, scalability and reliability
Decoupling — sender and receiver work independently; a UTM service can restart without losing telemetry
Load distribution — messages are processed in parallel by many consumers
Reliability — persistent storage of messages until they are consumed
Scalability — add consumers dynamically as traffic grows

title: JMS Architecture: Queues & Topics
desc: Two delivery models cover almost every messaging need

body.code:
Point-to-Point (Queue)              Publish-Subscribe (Topic)

Producer                             Publisher
   |                                     |
   v                                     v
[ QUEUE ] --> exactly one            [ TOPIC ] --> every subscriber
              consumer gets              |    \
              each message           Subscriber A  Subscriber B

clearance requests,                  position broadcasts,
work distribution                    airspace status updates

items: Message producer — sends messages to a queue or topic; message consumer — receives them
Message queue — waiting line for messages (point-to-point model)
Topic — broadcast model for multiple receivers (publish-subscribe)
Message types: Text, Bytes, Object, Map, Stream

title: Telemetry Through a Topic
desc: The backbone of the Module 4 reference system, in three annotations

body.code: // producer — the ingest handler from Module 8 publishes each accepted fix jmsTemplate.convertAndSend("telemetry.topic", fix.withDrone(droneId)); // consumer A — the live map (Module 14); durable: fixes wait for it while it restarts @JmsListener(destination = "telemetry.topic", containerFactory = "topicFactory", subscription = "live-map") void onFix(Fix fix) { mapService.update(fix); } // consumer B — conflict detection, same messages, independently @JmsListener(destination = "telemetry.topic", containerFactory = "topicFactory", subscription = "conflicts") void detect(Fix fix) { conflictEngine.feed(fix); } // the factory that makes it a topic — and makes the subscriptions survive a restart factory.setPubSubDomain(true); factory.setSubscriptionDurable(true); factory.setClientId("utm-backend");

items: The gateway doesn't know or care who listens — add a flight logger next week without touching it
The map can crash and restart — conflict detection keeps running; that isolation is the whole point

Durable subscription: without it, a topic delivers only to whoever is connected right now — the map restarts and the fixes from those 20 seconds are gone. With it, the broker keeps them for the named subscriber
Queue vs. topic is one flag in the factory — same annotation, different delivery semantics

title: Kafka: A Log, Not a Queue
desc: Same word "message" — a fundamentally different storage model

body.code:
Classic broker (ActiveMQ / RabbitMQ)     Kafka (distributed log)

Producer --> [ queue ] --> Consumer      Producer --> [ p0 | p1 | p2 ]  append-only
              consumed message                            ^
              is GONE — broker            Consumer reads at its own OFFSET
              tracks delivery              — and can REWIND and replay

smart broker, simple clients             simple broker, smart clients

body.card: What the log model buys you
items: Queues delete on acknowledge; Kafka retains messages (by time or size) — consumers just move an offset
Replay is the killer feature for telemetry: re-run yesterday's traffic through a new conflict detector — exactly what validation in Module 13 needs
Consumer groups give queue semantics on a log; a partition key of droneId gives per-drone ordering
The price: cluster operations — for a single lab service, a classic broker is the right size

title: Delivered Once? Pick Your Guarantee
desc: Every broker offers the same three promises — and 'exactly once' is mostly a consumer-side discipline

rows: A message is lost when the consumer dies mid-processing
Position fixes: the next one arrives in a second anyway
Consumer acknowledges after processing; broker redelivers if no ack
A message arrives twice when the ack is lost
Everything that matters — clearances, alerts, mission commands
Transactions spanning broker and database, or Kafka's idempotent producer + transactional consumer
Expensive, slow, and only inside one system's boundary
Rarely worth it — usually replaced by the line below

body.code: // at-least-once + an idempotent consumer = the practical "exactly once" @JmsListener(destination = "clearance.requests") // a QUEUE: one handler per request void handle(ClearanceRequest req) { if (repo.existsByRequestId(req.requestId())) return; // seen it — the redelivery is harmless zone.issueClearance(req); // Module 10's command side repo.save(req.requestId()); // same transaction as the clearance }

items: Process a clearance request twice without the guard and the drone holds two clearances for one mission — the second one conflicts with the first, and your own 409 fires against you
The key is the sender's: requestId for commands, droneId + ts for fixes — never the broker's message id, it changes on redelivery
Asynchronous messaging buys decoupling, buffering and fan-out — the sender never waits, the system never loses a message to a restart
Queue = work distribution (each message to exactly one consumer); topic = broadcast (every subscriber sees everything)
Pick the broker by guarantees, not fashion: ActiveMQ (the classic JMS broker), RabbitMQ (AMQP, JMS via plugin, flexible routing), Kafka (a distributed log, not JMS — replay and volume)
At-least-once + idempotent consumer is the practical 'exactly once'; a durable subscription is what keeps a topic's messages for a consumer that is restarting
Telemetry fan-out is a topic — map, logger and conflict detection subscribe independently
Clearance processing is a queue — exactly one handler must act on each request
Incident replay wants Kafka — rewind the offset and re-fly yesterday's airspace against new logic
